questions.stem:
Bag $\mathrm{A}$ contains 5 red, 4 yellow and 3 green beads.
Bag $\mathrm{B}$ only contains red and yellow beads.
A bead is selected at random from bag $\mathrm{A}$ and a second bead is selected at random from bag $\mathrm{B}$
Given that the probability that both beads selected are yellow is $\frac{3}{16}$

parts.label: a(i)
parts.text:
(a) (i) find the probability of selecting a yellow bead from bag $\mathrm{B}$
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a)(i) M1: for a suitable expression (in their $p$) for the probability both are yellow, e.g. $\mathrm{P}(YY) = \frac{4}{12} \times p$
A1: for correct probability of yellow from $\mathrm{B}$: $\frac{4}{12} \times p = \frac{3}{16}$ so $p = \frac{9}{16}$ (Allow 0.5625 and condone 0.563). Can be implied by values on tree diagram.

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.text:
(ii) Hence complete the tree diagram below by finding the probability on each branch.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a)(ii) B1: for a correct 1st column of tree diagram (probabilities from $\mathrm{A}$)
B1ft: (dep on M1 in (i)) for correct 2nd column of tree diagram (ft their $\frac{9}{16}$ and $1-\frac{9}{16}$)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Find the exact probability that at least one of the two beads selected is yellow.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: for selection of all correct cases (including the $1-$ if required), e.g. $\mathrm{P}(RY)+\mathrm{P}(Y)+\mathrm{P}(GY)$ or $1-\mathrm{P}(RR)-\mathrm{P}(GR)$ or $\mathrm{P}(\ldots Y)+\mathrm{P}(YR)$. Don't need $\mathrm{P}(\ldots$ may be implied by correct probability products seen (ft their tree diagram)
A1ft: for a correct complete probability expression (ft their tree diagram) or awrt 0.708. Must see product pairs (for ft) or implied by correct values, e.g. $\frac{15}{64}+\frac{7}{48}+\frac{3}{16}+\frac{9}{64}$. May see $1-\mathrm{P}(\overline{Y}\,\overline{Y})$ (M1) and $1-\frac{2}{3}\times"\frac{7}{16}"$ (A1ft), e.g. $\frac{5}{12}\times"\frac{9}{16}"+\frac{4}{12}+\frac{3}{12}\times"\frac{9}{16}"$ or $1-\left[\frac{5}{12}\times"\frac{7}{16}"+\frac{3}{12}\times"\frac{7}{16}"\right]$ or $"\frac{9}{16}"+\frac{1}{3}\times"\frac{7}{16}"$
A1: for an exact answer $=\frac{136}{192}=\frac{17}{24}=0.708\dot{3}$; fraction needn't be simplified but decimal must have $\dot{3}$

parts.label: c
parts.text:
The event $X$ is that at least one of the beads selected is yellow.
The event $W$ is that a green bead is selected.
(c) Find the exact value of $\mathrm{P}(W \mid X)$
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) M1: for a correct ratio of probabilities expression (in symbols) $\left[\mathrm{P}(W \mid X) = \right] \frac{\mathrm{P}(W \cap X)}{\mathrm{P}(X)}$ or $\frac{\frac{3}{12}\times"\frac{9}{16}"}{"(b)"}$ or ft their values seen
A1: for an exact answer $=\frac{27}{136}$. NB an answer of awrt 0.199 (0.198529411\ldots) implies M1.
Acc: If scored 2nd A0 in (b) for 0.708 (or better) then allow A1 in (c) for awrt 0.199

questions.stem:
Runners in an athletics club can train with either coach $A$ or coach $B$ for the $400\,\mathrm{m}$ race.
Coach $A$ trains 120 runners for the $400\,\mathrm{m}$ and records the best time, $x$ seconds, for each runner.
The results are summarised by the following statistics
$\sum x = 6612 \qquad \sum x^2 = 364902$

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Calculate the mean of the best times for the runners trained by coach $A$
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: (a) B1: $\left[\bar{x} = \frac{6612}{120}\right] = 55.1$ (seconds), or $55\frac{1}{10}$ only (may be seen in the question). ISW e.g. 55.1 followed by 55 etc. Do not accept $\frac{551}{10}$ that scores B0

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Calculate the standard deviation of the best times for the runners trained by coach $A$
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: $\left[\sigma_x = \right] \sqrt{\frac{364902}{120} - ("55.1")^2}$ or $\sqrt{4.84}$; for a correct expression (values seen not just a formula) (including $\sqrt{\ }$)
A1: $= 2.2$ (seconds) or $\frac{11}{5}$ o.e. (allow $s = 2.209\ldots$ so awrt 2.21). Correct answer is 2 marks

parts.label: c
parts.text:
The mean and standard deviation for the best times of the 100 runners trained for the $400\,\mathrm{m}$ by coach $B$ are 55.1 seconds and 3.6 seconds respectively.
A $400\,\mathrm{m}$ race consists of equal numbers of the fastest runners trained by coach $A$ and by coach $B$
(c) State, giving a reason, which coach is more likely to have trained the winner.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) Ignore comments about different number of runners. Don't need to state means are the same. If there is no answer given for (b) then no marks can be scored in (c).
"2.2"<3.6: M1: for coach $B$ and states s.d. of $B$ is greater o.e. Must compare. Allow implied choose $B$, e.g. $B$ has a greater range or $B$'s values are more spread out or $3.6 > "2.2"$ or $\sigma_B > "2.2"$. May say s.d. of $A$ is smaller which is equivalent to saying s.d. of $B$ is larger
dB1: (dep on 1st B1 scored) for clear reason why greater s.d. means choose coach $B$. Idea of greater range and more extreme values (faster times) in $B$, e.g. $B$ has more (or greater chance of or greater \% of) runners at lower times (may compare mean $-$ 1 or 2 or 3 standard deviations to show that $B$ has the quicker time), e.g. coach $A$ (52.9) > (51.5) coach $B$ so coach $B$ likely to be quickest
NB "coach $B$ since $B$ has greater range/s.d. and so more extreme values" scores B1B1
SC "2.2">3.6 (A0 in (b) and answer > 3.6): B1: equivalent reasons as above but choose $A$; dB1: same rules as above but applied to $A$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- Coach $B$ because standard deviation is greater M1
- This means $B$ has a greater range and therefore more extreme values A1ft

questions.stem:
A manufacturer makes components for the car industry.
On average 1.5\% of the components made are defective.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Using a suitable model, find the probability that in a random sample of 36 components there are
(i) exactly 2 defective components,
(ii) more than 3 defective components.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) M1: for selecting $\mathrm{B}(36, 0.015)$; sight of or use of. Must be $\mathrm{B}(\ldots)$ [Implied by sight of $\mathrm{Po}(0.54)$]. May be implied by sight of: 0.0848 or awrt 0.085 or 0.00203 or 0.998 or 0.002. $[\text{Let } D = \text{the number of defective components}] \ D \sim \mathrm{B}(36, 0.015)$
(i) A1: $\left[\mathrm{P}(D=2) = \right] 0.084792\ldots$ awrt 0.0848
(ii) A1: $\left[\mathrm{P}(D>3) = 1-\mathrm{P}(D \leqslant 3) = 1-0.9979\ldots = \right] 0.002032\ldots$ awrt 0.00203 [Allow $2.03\times10^{-3}$]
Use of Poisson $\mathrm{Po}(0.54)$: (i) $0.08496$ scores A0; (ii) $0.002309\ldots$ awrt 0.00231 scores A1
Notation: We do not accept "calculator speak" e.g. $N=36, p=0.015$ instead of $\mathrm{B}(36, 0.015)$

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Once every six months, the manufacturer tests whether the proportion of defective components has changed using hypotheses $\mathrm{H}_0 : p = 0.015$ and $\mathrm{H}_1 : p \neq 0.015$
A random sample of 260 components is taken and 8 are found to be defective.
(b) Using a 5\% level of significance, complete the test.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: for sight of $\mathrm{B}(260, 0.015)$; may be implied by probability of awrt 0.0441 or awrt 0.0264 or awrt 0.956, or correct CR $X=0$ [or $\leqslant 0$] and $X \geqslant 9$, or $\mathrm{P}(X \geqslant 8) = 0.04$ or better. $[\text{Let } X = \text{the number of defective components}] \ X \sim \mathrm{B}(260, 0.015)$
A1: for probability of awrt 0.0441 (selected if more probabilities seen), condone $\mathrm{P}(X=8)=0.0441\ldots$. If $\mathrm{P}(X \geqslant 8)$ is explicitly seen allow 0.04 or better, or for the correct CR $X=0$ [or $\leqslant 0$] and $X \geqslant 9$. Allow acceptance region $[1,8]$ (o.e.). $\left[\mathrm{P}(X \geqslant 8) = \right] 0.0441(1\ldots)$
A1: dep on M1A1 for a correct conclusion in context. Allow e.g. proportion/probability of defective components has not changed; proportion/probability of defective components is still 0.015; allow "defectives" instead of "components". If a comparison is seen (other than $0.956 < 0.975$) it must be within 0.025. Incorrect comparisons score A0 (condone missing comparison). Do not accept contradictory statements e.g. "significant so insufficient evidence of change in proportion" would score A0. "Insufficient evidence that $p \neq 0.015$" is A0, we need the words. $[0.04 > 0.025$ so not significant$]$ Insufficient evidence that proportion/probability of defective components has changed (o.e.)
SC Poisson Approximation (If you see $\mathrm{Po}(3.9)$ or probability $0.0454\ldots$): B2 and mark as M0A1A1. B1: for probability of awrt 0.0454 or 0.04\ldots if $\mathrm{P}(X \geqslant 8)$ seen or CR as above. B1: for correct conclusion in context (same rules as above)

questions.stem:
Kay is studying the variables Daily Total Sunshine ($x$) and Daily Total Rainfall ($y$) from the large data set for Leeming in 2015
Kay starts with 5th May and then selects every 10th day thereafter.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) State the name of the sampling technique Kay uses.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: (a) B1: Systematic (sampling). Ignore other non-contradictory descriptions. Condone misspelling. If a clear choice is given e.g. stratified or systematic we take the final answer.
parts.notes: LDS convention (spec other_requirements: large data set)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Kay wants to find the regression line of $y$ on $x$ for these data.
(b) Using your knowledge of the large data set, explain how Kay might need to clean these data before finding the equation of the regression line.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: (b) B1: The (Daily Total) Rainfall data may contain "tr" entries (these will need a suitable value substituted before calculations can take place). For mention of "tr" or "trace" entries in rain(fall) [or $y$] data. Ignore "n/a". Ignore any comment about what to do with trace.
parts.notes: LDS convention (spec other_requirements: large data set)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
The equation of the regression line Kay finds is $y = 0.741 + 0.199x$
(c) Using your knowledge of the large data set,
(i) state the units of the gradient of the regression line,
(ii) give an interpretation of the $y$-intercept of the regression line.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c)(i) B1: mm/h (o.e.) e.g. $\mathrm{mm\,h^{-1}}$ or $\mathrm{mm\,hrs^{-1}}$ or $\frac{\text{mm}}{\text{hours}}$; for mm/h or equivalent in words.
(c)(ii) B1: When there is no sun(shine) there is (on average) 0.7(41) (mm) of rain, or the amount of rain when there is no sun(shine) (o.e.); for the idea of amount of rain when no sun. "Minimum rain" is B0. Don't need value or units but if given must be correct or consistent with (i)

parts.label: d
parts.text:
Kay's teacher claimed that the greater the amount of sunshine in a day the lower the amount of rain there should be.
(d) State, giving a reason, whether the teacher's claim is true for Kay's data.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: (d) B1: e.g. Not consistent (since); Kay's line says positive correlation, or gradient or regression coefficient or regression line or 0.199 is positive; for a suitable reason and saying not consistent (o.e.) e.g. "false" or "untrue" or "no". Reason only needs to be about the line and may be a description e.g. as $x$ increases $y$ increases, or at least 2 values of $x$ substituted and $y$ values evaluated

parts.label: e
parts.text:
The teacher used all the data for these variables from the large data set for Leeming in 2015, as a sample.
The teacher calculated the product moment correlation coefficient for $x$ and $y$ to be $-0.160$
In a suitable test to determine whether there is evidence to support the teacher's claim, the $p$-value was 0.015
(e) Using a 5\% level of significance, state the hypotheses and conclusion for this test.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(e) B1: $\mathrm{H}_0 : \rho = 0$ and $\mathrm{H}_1 : \rho < 0$; for both hypotheses correct in terms of $\rho$ (condone attempt at $\rho$ that looks like $p$)
B1: $[p\text{-value} < 5\% \text{ so significant result}]$ there is evidence to support the teacher's claim; for a correct conclusion in context with no contradiction. Using words "support" and "teacher's claim" or "negative correlation" and "sun or $x$" and "rain or $y$" [If a comparison is given it must be $0.015 < 0.05$]

parts.label: f
parts.text:
(f) For the test in part (e) describe
(i) the sample,
(ii) a possible population.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(f)(i) B1: The sample is rainfall ($y$) and sunshine ($x$) for May~Oct in (Leeming) in 2015; for recognising that all the data/days for these variables in LDS for 2015 is the sample. Condone omitting "Leeming". B0 for "sunshine and rainfall for Leeming in 2015". It could be the population.
(f)(ii) B1: e.g. (rainfall and sunshine) for: (Leeming) for all of 2015, or Leeming anytime (not just May~Oct), or Leeming for May~October for other years too, or May~Oct in UK etc; for a suitable attempt to describe a population. The teacher's sample must be a subset.

(f)(ii) B1: e.g. (rainfall and sunshine) for: (Leeming) for all of 2015, or Leeming anytime (not just May~Oct), or Leeming for May~October for other years too, or May~Oct in UK etc; for a suitable attempt to describe a population. The teacher's sample must be a subset.

questions.stem:
The heights of men in a tennis club are normally distributed with a mean of $183\,\mathrm{cm}$ and a standard deviation of $4.9\,\mathrm{cm}$.
A man from the tennis club is selected at random.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the probability that the man's height is
(i) more than $186\,\mathrm{cm}$,
(ii) between $175\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $185\,\mathrm{cm}$.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a)(i) B1: $[\text{Let } M \text{ be the height of a man from the club, } \mathrm{P}(M>186) = ] 0.270187\ldots = $ awrt 0.270
(a)(ii) B1: $[\mathrm{P}(175<M<185) = ] 0.6071520\ldots = $ awrt 0.607

parts.label: b
parts.text:
The heights of women in the tennis club are normally distributed with a mean of $\mu\,\mathrm{cm}$ and a standard deviation of $\sigma\,\mathrm{cm}$.
Given that 40\% of the women are shorter than $170\,\mathrm{cm}$ and 15\% are taller than $175\,\mathrm{cm}$,
(b) find the value of $\mu$ and the value of $\sigma$
Show your working clearly.
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) $[\text{Let } F \text{ be the height of a women from the club}]$
M1: $\mathrm{P}(F<170) = 0.40 \Rightarrow \frac{170-\mu}{\sigma} = -0.2533$ [calc gives $-0.253347\ldots$]; for standardising 170 with $\mu$ and $\sigma$ and set equal to a $z$ value $0<|z|<0.3$
M1: $\mathrm{P}(F>175) = 0.15 \Rightarrow \frac{175-\mu}{\sigma} = 1.0364$ [calc gives $1.036433\ldots$]; for standardising 175 with $\mu$ and $\sigma$ and set equal to a $z$ value $1<|z|<2$
M1: Solving: $5 = \sigma(1.0364+0.2533)$; for solving their 2 linear equations, reducing to a linear equation in one variable. This can be implied by two answers that are correct to 2sf. To award the A marks they must have scored 1st M1 and 2nd M1
A1: $\sigma = 3.87687\ldots$ awrt 3.88
A1: $\mu = 170.9820\ldots$ awrt 171 (Must not be from incorrect working e.g. $\sigma<0$)
Ans only: We need to see the linear equations in $\mu$ and $\sigma$ to start awarding marks. If 1st M1 and 2nd M1 are scored and correct answers are seen we can award 5 marks.
MR: (15\% as 0.015) 2nd M1 for $z=2.17\ldots$, 3rd M1 implied by $\sigma=2.06\ldots$ and $\mu=170.5\ldots$ i.e. Maximum M1M1M1A0A0

parts.label: c
parts.text:
A man from the tennis club and a woman from the tennis club are selected at random.
(c) Find the probability that both players have heights between $170\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $175\,\mathrm{cm}$.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) M1: $[\mathrm{P}(170<F<175) = ] 1-(0.40+0.15) = 0.45$ (allow awrt 0.45); $[\mathrm{P}(170<M<175) = ] 0.047282\ldots = $ (allow awrt 0.047); for correct probability for women or correct probability for men, or clear intention to multiply $\mathrm{P}(170<F<175)$ by $\mathrm{P}(170<M<175)$
A1ft: $[\mathrm{P}(170<F<175) \times \mathrm{P}(170<M<175) = ] "0.45" \times "0.047"$ or $0.021\ldots$; for using $\mathrm{P}(170<F<175) \times \mathrm{P}(170<M<175)$ with one probability correct to 2sf
A1: So $\mathrm{P}(\text{both}) = 0.021277\ldots$ awrt 0.021. Correct answer only is 3 marks.
MR (if used in (b)): $\mathrm{P}(170<F<175) = 0.585$ (or awrt 0.58 or 0.59) answer awrt 0.027 or 0.028. All 3 marks can be scored here.

questions.stem:
The discrete random variable $R$ takes even integer values from 2 to $2n$ inclusive.
The probability distribution of $R$ is given by
$\mathrm{P}(R=r) = \frac{r}{k} \qquad r = 2, 4, 6, \ldots, 2n$
where $k$ is a constant.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Show that $k = n(n+1)$
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) M1: Use sum of probs $=1$: $1 = \frac{1}{k}(2+4+\ldots+2n)$. Allow $1 = \frac{S_r}{k}$ where $S_r = \sum_{r=1}^{n} 2r$; for clear attempt/intention to use sum of probs $=1$ for $n$ terms. Must see $k$ and "$=1$". Condone missing $\ldots$; $\sum_{2}^{2n} r$ is M0 since not $n$ terms
M1: Sum e.g. $\frac{n}{2}[4+2(n-1)]$ or $\frac{n}{2}[2+2n]$ or use $\sum_{1}^{n} r = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}$; for using an arithmetic series or $\Sigma r$ to find sum to $n$ terms. No need for $k$
A1: Use sum formula: e.g. $1 = \frac{1}{k}\times\frac{n}{2}[4+2(n-1)]$ or $1 = \frac{n}{2}\left[\frac{2}{k}+\frac{2n}{k}\right]$; (dep on M1M1) for a correct working leading to a correct equation in $k$ and $n$
A1*cso: $k = n(n+1) \ *$; cso for correct solution with both Ms clearly scored and no incorrect working seen
SC: Start with $1 = \frac{n}{k}\left[\frac{2}{k}+\frac{2n}{k}\right]$ or $1 = \frac{1}{k}\times\frac{n}{2}[4+2(n-1)]$ and no mention of $a$ and $l$ or $a$ and $d$. Score SC B2 (M1M0A1A0) 1st B1 for the start and 2nd B1cso for completing to printed answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
When $n = 20$
(b) find the exact value of $\mathrm{P}(16 \leqslant R < 26)$
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) M1: Cases: $R = 16, 18, 20, 22$ and $24$; for identifying the correct values of $R$
A1: Probability $= \left[\frac{16+18+20+22+24}{20\times21}\right] = \frac{5}{21}$; for a correct probability (any exact equivalent) allow $0.238095\ldots$. Correct answer with no working scores 2 marks

parts.label: c
parts.text:
When $n = 20$, a random value $g$ of $R$ is taken and the quadratic equation in $x$
$x^2 + gx + 3g = 5$
is formed.
(c) Find the exact probability that the equation has no real roots.
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) M1: $[\text{No real roots} \Rightarrow \Delta<0]$ so $g^2-4(3g-5)[<0]$; for attempt to use discriminant [$<0$ not needed here]. Condone $g^2-12g$
M1: $\left[g^2-12g+20<0 \Rightarrow\right] (g-10)(g-2)[<0]$; for attempting to factorise or find critical values for their 3TQ (ignore their $<$ \& allow $=0$)
M1: So require $2<g<10$ or $4 \leqslant g \leqslant 8$; for choosing the correct (inside) region, ft their critical values from a 3TQ with $<0$
dM1: So require $g = 4, 6, 8$ only; (dep on 3rd M1) for choosing/identifying the appropriate values of $g$ (ft their critical values from 3TQ with $<0$ used)
A1: Probability $= \left[\frac{4+6+8}{20\times21}\right] = \frac{18}{420} = \frac{3}{70}$; for an exact probability in any form. Allow $0.0428571\ldots$. A correct answer with no incorrect working will score full marks.
Acc: If scored A0 for an answer of awrt 0.238 in (b), allow A1 in (c) for awrt 0.0429
